newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian stocks rebound cautiously from last week.
newsitem.headline: Asian stocks rebound cautiously from last week.

text.p: Asian stocks on Monday clawed back some of the ground lost in a correction last week that was sparked by fears the U.S. central bank was about to clamp down on ebullient markets.
Japan's Nikkei 225 surged 327.01 points, or 1.61 percent, to close at 20,603.71, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index put on 41.50 points to end at 13,144.23, or 0.32 percent higher.
Stock prices also climbed in Australia, Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Taiwan.

Steep declines on Friday were blamed on the reaction to comments by Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan. Investors were buying again on Monday because of a better U.S. inflation outlook and the opportunity to pick up bargains, traders said.
But trading volume was thin throughout Asia as investors appeared uncertain what the markets will do next.
"It seems the Asian markets overreacted to the Fed chairman's comments," said Yasuo Ueki, general manager at Nikko Securities Co. Ltd. "But a recovery to the pre-plunge level will be gradual..."
On Friday, Asian markets led a worldwide slide in stock prices as the first to react to Greenspan's remarks in a speech on Thursday night.
The Fed chief spoke of "irrational exuberance" infecting markets and said the direction of inflation was impossible to determine.

Asian markets took his remarks as a signal that the U.S. central bank would raise interest rates. Losses on the Nikkei were the sharpest since April 1995, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng index suffered its biggest one-day fall in about nine months.
But the reaction in the United States was more moderate. The Dow Jones index of 30 industrials clawed back from a 140-point drop to finish down 55 points on Friday.
"It was only natural that the Nikkei average rebounded since the U.S. markets' losses were not that big," Harushige Kobayashi, Yamaichi Securities deputy general manager, said on Monday.
Malaysian stocks rebounded with buyers picking up stocks cheapened by Friday's fall, traders said. The benchmark Composite Index closed up 12.04 points, or 1.01 percent, to 1,203.36.

Thai share prices, which moved in a narrow range and negative levels for most of the day, closed up 1.43 percent in a technical rebound, brokers said. The SET index gained 12.57 points to end at 889.46.
Singapore shares ended steady in light trade, closing up 8.09 points at 2,198.48. Dealers said the market was underpinned by a reassuring figures on U.S. inflation.
U.S. unemployment data for November, released on Friday, were weaker than expected, opening the way for a recovery by U.S. Treasuries.
"This helped to reassure the market that a (U.S.) rate hike is quite unlikely," one Singapore dealer said.
Australian shares bounced to a firmer close, ending 25.9 points, or 1.12 percent higher, at 2,339.8 while Taipei stocks inched up 29.22 points, or 0.43 percent, to 6,808.83.

Seoul shares, however, gave up early gains to end at a new three-year low on fears of labour strife and share oversupply, traders said. The composite index fell 3.94 points, or 0.57 percent, to a provisional close of 692.17.
